01.r: Sets the scene: the time of harvest.
01.n: Literally 'and in your reaping': an infinitive with 'in' and 'your', which Hebrew uses for 'when you'. YLT keeps that shape. Gesenius gives the verb's first sense as TO CUT OFF, especially grain.

02.r: Marks 'the harvest of your land' as the object of 'reap'.
02.n: This small word marks a definite direct object and has no English equivalent; it is counted here with 'the harvest of'.

03.n: The noun comes from the same root as the verb before it: 'in your reaping the reaping of your land'. The DRC's 'corn' meant grain in older English.

04.n: The 'your' here is plural, addressing the people together; from the next clause on the law speaks to each one as 'you' singular.

06.r: Do not carry the reaping through to the very end of the field.
06.n: Gesenius gives the base sense as to be completed, finished; BDB gives this form as complete, bring to an end. The KJV's 'make clean riddance' and Geneva's 'rid cleane' take it as clearing the field entirely.
t: you shall ... cut it to the very ground

07.r: The outer strip of the field, left standing.
07.n: Gesenius gives first a quarter of the heavens, then side, region; BDB gives corner, side. 'Edge' suits a strip along the field's border; the KJV's 'corners' is the traditional rendering.

09.n: Literally 'in your reaping', now with 'your' singular. Where Leviticus 19:9 has 'to reap' after 'finish', this verse has 'in your reaping'; otherwise the two laws run word for word alike up to this point.

10.r: The stalks that fall or are missed by the reapers.
10.n: BDB and the brief's lexicon give simply 'gleaning'. The noun shares its consonants with the verb 'gather' that follows. Geneva's 'aftergathering' describes it well.

13.r: Do not go back to pick up what lies on the ground.
13.n: Gesenius: to gather, to collect, properly things lying on the ground, such as ears of grain.

14.r: Someone without the means to live without help.
14.n: Gesenius gives afflicted, wretched, poor, often with the added idea of piety; BDB adds 'oppressed by rich and powerful'.

15.r: Someone living in Israel who was not born into it.
15.n: Gesenius: a sojourner, stranger, foreigner, a person living out of his own country. BDB: a temporary dweller, a newcomer with no inherited rights.

16.r: Leave the edge and the gleaning for these two to take.
16.n: Gesenius gives the first sense as to loosen bands, to let go. BDB notes that with 'to' before a person, as here, it means to leave something to that person's possession.

17.r: The unreaped edge and the gleaning.

18.r: God speaks in his own person and gives the law his authority.
18.n: Hebrew has no 'am' here; the clause is verbless, 'I the LORD your God'. YLT places 'am' later: 'I Jehovah am your God'.

19.r: The personal name of Israel's God.

20.r: The God of the whole people.
20.n: The form is plural but the meaning is singular. The 'your' is plural, though the commands before it address each Israelite as 'you' singular.

01.n: θερίζω, 'to reap'. Where Leviticus 19:9 has the compound ἐκθερίζω, this verse has the plain verb.

07.n: τὸ λοιπὸν τοῦ θερισμοῦ, 'the rest of the harvest', where the Hebrew has 'the edge of'. The Greek does not name the edge.

09.n: ἐν τῷ θερίζειν σε, 'in your reaping', matching the Hebrew form exactly.

10.n: τὰ ἀποπίπτοντα, 'the things that fall off'.

17.n: The Greek has 'it', singular, where the Hebrew has 'them'.

18.n: The Greek here has no 'am': ἐγὼ κύριος, 'I the Lord'.
